speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Good afternoon.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: My colleagues and I remain squarely focused on achieving our dual-mandate goals of maximum employment and stable prices for the benefit of the American people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Despite heightened uncertainty, the economy is still in a solid position.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The unemployment rate remains low, and the labor market is at or near maximum employment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Inflation has come down a great deal but has been running somewhat above our 2 percent longer-run objective.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In support of our goals, today the Federal Open Market Committee decided to leave our policy interest rate unchanged.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The risks of higher unemployment and higher inflation appear to have risen, and we believe that the current stance of monetary policy leaves us well positioned to respond in a timely way to potential economic developments.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I will have more to say about monetary policy after briefly reviewing economic developments.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: [Cough] Pardon me.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Following growth of 2.5 percent last year, GDP was reported to have edged down in the first quarter, reflecting swings in net exports that were likely driven by businesses bringing in imports ahead of potential tariffs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: This unusual swing complicated GDP measurement last quarter.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Private domestic final purchases, or PDFP—which excludes net exports, inventory investment, and government spending—grew at a solid 3 percent rate in the first quarter, the same as last year’s pace.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Within PDFP, growth of consumer spending moderated while investment in equipment and intangibles rebounded from weakness in the fourth quarter.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Surveys of households and businesses, however, report a sharp decline in sentiment and elevated uncertainty about the economic outlook, largely reflecting trade policy concerns.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It remains to be seen how these developments might affect future spending and investment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In the labor market, conditions have remained solid.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Payroll job gains averaged 155,000 per month over the past three months.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The unemployment rate, at 4.2 percent, remains low and has stayed in a narrow range for the past year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Wage growth has continued to moderate, while still outpacing inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Overall, a wide set of indicators suggests that conditions in the labor market are broadly in balance and consistent with maximum employment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The labor market is not a source of significant inflationary pressures.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Inflation has eased significantly from its highs in mid-2022 but remains somewhat elevated relative to our 2 percent longer-run goal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Total PCE prices rose 2.3 percent over the 12 months ending in March; excluding the volatile food and energy categories, core PCE prices rose 2.6 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Near-term measures of inflation expectations have moved up, as reflected in both market- and survey-based measures.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Survey respondents, including consumers, businesses, and professional forecasters, point to tariffs as the driving factor.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Beyond the next year or so, however, most measures of longer-term expectations remain consistent with our 2 percent inflation goal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Our monetary policy actions are guided by our dual mandate to promote maximum employment and stable prices for the American people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: At today’s meeting, the Committee decided to maintain the target range for the federal funds rate at 4¼ to 4½ percent and to continue reducing the size of the balance sheet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The new Administration is in the process of implementing substantial policy changes in four distinct areas: trade, immigration, fiscal policy, and regulation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The tariff increases announced so far have been significantly larger than anticipated.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: All of these policies are still evolving, however, and their effects on the economy remain highly uncertain.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: As economic conditions evolve, we’ll continue to determine the appropriate stance of monetary policy based on the incoming data, the outlook, and the balance of risks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If the large increases in tariffs that have been announced are sustained, they are likely to generate a rise in inflation, a slowdown in economic growth, and an increase in unemployment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The effects on inflation could be short lived, reflecting a one-time shift in the price level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It is also possible that the inflationary effects could instead be more persistent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Avoiding that outcome will depend on the size of the tariffs’ effect—tariff effects, on how long it takes for them to pass through fully into prices, and, ultimately, on keeping longer-term inflation expectations well anchored.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Our obligation is to keep longer-term inflation expectations well anchored and to prevent a one-time increase in the price level from becoming an ongoing inflation problem.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: As we act to meet that obligation, we’ll balance our maximum-employment and price-stability mandates, keeping in mind that, without price stability, we cannot achieve the long periods of strong labor market conditions that benefit all Americans.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We may find ourselves in the challenging scenario in which our dual-mandate goals are in tension.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If that were to occur, we would consider how far the economy is from each goal, and the potentially different time horizons over which those respective gaps would be anticipated to close.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: For the time being, we’re well positioned to wait for greater clarity before considering any adjustments to our policy stance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: At this meeting, the Committee continued its discussions as part of our five-year review of our monetary policy framework.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We focused on inflation dynamics and the implications for our monetary policy strategy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Our review includes outreach and public events involving a wide range of parties, including Fed Listens events around the country and a research conference next week.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Throughout this process, we’re open to new ideas and critical feedback, and we will take on board lessons of the last five years in determining our findings.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We intend to wrap up the review by late summer.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The Fed has been assigned two goals for monetary policy—maximum employment and stable prices.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We remain committed to supporting maximum employment, bringing inflation sustainably to our 2 percent goal, and keeping longer-term inflation expectations well anchored.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Our success in delivering on these goals matters to all Americans.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We understand that our actions affect communities, families, and businesses across the country.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Everything we do is in service to our public mission.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We at the Fed will do everything we can to achieve our maximum-employment and price-stability goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Thank you.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I look forward to your questions.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Steve.

speaker: STEVE LIESMAN
sentence: Steve Liesman, CNBC.

speaker: STEVE LIESMAN
sentence: Thank you, Mr.

speaker: STEVE LIESMAN
sentence: Chair, for taking my question.

speaker: STEVE LIESMAN
sentence: A lot has happened since the last meeting.

speaker: STEVE LIESMAN
sentence: There have been tariffs put on, tariffs taken off, and meanwhile, there was a bill advancing in Congress.

speaker: STEVE LIESMAN
sentence: And I just wonder if I could press you on the last part of your statement.

speaker: STEVE LIESMAN
sentence: Are you any closer now to deciding which side of the mandate is going to need urgent care first?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Well, so, as we noted in our—in our statement—postmeeting statement, we’ve judged that the risks to higher employment and higher inflation have both risen.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And this, by the way, of course, is compared to March.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s what we can say.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I don’t think we can say, you know, which way this will shake out.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think there’s a great deal of uncertainty about, for example, where tariff policies are going to, to settle out and also, when they do settle out, what will be the implications for the economy for growth and for employment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think it’s too early to know that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, I mean, ultimately, we think our policy rate is in—is in a good place to stay as we await further clarity on tariffs and, ultimately, their implications for the economy.

speaker: STEVE LIESMAN
sentence: Hearing you describe what you’re looking for in terms of being able to make a decision, it sounded like that’s a long-term process before you sound like you’re going to be comfortable, or the Committee would be comfortable, to act on what the data’s telling you.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I don’t think we know.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, I think—look where we are today.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We have an economy that, if you “look through,” you know, the sort of distortions in Q1 GDP, you’ve still got an economy that looks like it’s growing at a solid pace.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The labor market appears to be solid.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Inflation is running just a bit above 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So it’s an economy that’s been resilient and is in good shape, and our policy is sort of modestly or moderately restrictive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s 100 basis points less restrictive than it was last fall.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so we think that leaves us in a good place to wait and see.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We don’t think we need to be in a hurry.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We think we can be patient.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re going to be watching the data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The data may move quickly or slowly, but we do think we’re in a good position, where we are, to, to let things evolve and become clearer in terms of what should be the monetary policy response.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Nick.

speaker: NICK TIMIRAOS
sentence: Nick Timiraos for the Wall Street Journal.

speaker: NICK TIMIRAOS
sentence: Chair Powell, there’s naturally a lot of [inaudible] around 2021 in supply shocks.

speaker: NICK TIMIRAOS
sentence: But there are some who argue that the current situation has notable differences.

speaker: NICK TIMIRAOS
sentence: Energy costs are down.

speaker: NICK TIMIRAOS
sentence: Housing imbalances look nothing like they did four years ago.

speaker: NICK TIMIRAOS
sentence: Labor demand appears to be gradually cooling, with wage growth running below 4 percent.

speaker: NICK TIMIRAOS
sentence: What do you see right now that could nourish higher inflation beyond a rise in goods prices this year?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think the underlying inflation picture is, is good.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s what you see, which is inflation now running a bit above 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we’ve had basically decent readings in housing services and nonhousing services, which is a big part of it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that part, I think is, is moving along well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But there’s just so much that we don’t know.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think—and we’re in a good position to wait and see, is the thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We don’t have to be in a hurry.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The economy is—has been resilient and is doing fairly well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Our policy is well positioned.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The costs of waiting to see further are fairly low, we think.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s what we’re doing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, you know, we’ll, we’ll see.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The Administration is entering into negotiations with many countries over tariffs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’ll know more with each week and month that goes by where—about where tariffs are going to land—you know, land, and we’ll know what the effects will be when we start to see those things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we think we’ll be learning.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I can’t tell you how long it will take.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, for now, it does seem like it’s, it’s, it’s a fairly clear decision for us to wait and see and watch.

speaker: NICK TIMIRAOS
sentence: So when you say that you don’t need to be in a hurry, does that mean that—could the outlook change in such a way that a change in your stance could be warranted as soon as your next meeting?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, as I said, we’re—we are comfortable with our policy stance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We think the right—we’re in the right place to wait and see how things evolve.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We don’t feel like we need to be in a hurry.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We feel like it’s appropriate to be patient.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, you know, when things develop—of course, we have a record of—we can move quickly when that’s appropriate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But we think right now, the appropriate thing to do is to wait and see how things evolve.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: There’s so much uncertainty.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If you talk to businesses or market participants or forecasters, everyone is just—is just waiting to see how developments play out, and then we’ll be able to make a better assessment of what the appropriate path for monetary policy is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we’re not in that place, and, you know, as that develops—and I can’t really give you a time frame on that.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Jonnelle.

speaker: JONNELLE MARTE
sentence: Jonnelle Marte with Bloomberg.

speaker: JONNELLE MARTE
sentence: So, many economists have been pricing in higher odds of a recession, and several are noting that it is more difficult for the Fed to cut rates preemptively, given the higher risks for higher inflation.

speaker: JONNELLE MARTE
sentence: So, given the outlook, do you still see a path for a soft landing, and what does that look like?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Well, let me say—I mean, so let’s, let’s, let’s look back and see where we are.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, go through 2024 up to the [present] day.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’ve had—we’ve had, you know, unemployment in the low 4s for more than a year, we’ve had inflation coming down in the—now in the mid-to-low 2s, and we’ve had an economy growing at 2½ percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that is—that is the economy as we see it now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: What looks likely, given the scope and scale of the tariffs, is that we will see the—certainly, the risks to higher inflation, higher unemployment have increased.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And if that’s what we do see, if—and if the tariffs are ultimately put in place at those levels, which we don’t know, then, then we will see—we won’t see further progress toward our goals, but we might see a delay in that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think in the—you know, in our thinking, we would get—we would never—we never do anything but keep achieving those goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But what we would—at least for the next, let’s say, year, we would—we would not be making progress toward those goals, again, if that is—if that’s the way the tariffs shake out.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The thing is, we don’t know that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: There’s so much uncertainty about the scale, scope, timing, and persistence of the tariffs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In terms of preemption, you know, I think you can look back at the 2019 cuts as preemptive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I wouldn’t say that what we did last fall was at all preemptive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If anything, it was a little late.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But 2019, we did cut three times.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But the situation was, you had a weakening economy, and you had inflation at 1.6 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s a situation where you can move preemptively.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Now we have inflation running above target.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It has been above target for four years.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s not so far above target now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we have an expectation conditional on what happens that we’ll see upward pressure on inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If you look at where forecasters are, they’re all forecasting an increase in inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So it makes it—and then we’ve also got, you know, forecasts of weakening in the economy, and some have recession forecasts.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We don’t make a—we don’t make—publish a forecast about, about that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We don’t publish a forecast that assesses how likely a recession is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, in any case, it’s not a situation where we can be preemptive, because we actually don’t know what the right response to, to the data will be until we see more data.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Colby.

speaker: COLBY SMITH
sentence: Colby Smith with the New York Times.

speaker: COLBY SMITH
sentence: How much weakness does the Committee need to see, though, in the labor market and the economy more broadly to lower interest rates again?

speaker: COLBY SMITH
sentence: Is it about a certain increase in the unemployment rate over a period of time, or perhaps a certain number of negative monthly job reports?

speaker: COLBY SMITH
sentence: I mean, how are you making that assessment?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, so first of all, we don’t see that yet, right?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We have 4.2 percent unemployment, good participation, wages behaving very well, participation, I mentioned, at a good level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, you know, with the labor market, we would look at the totality of the—of the data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’d look at the level of the unemployment rate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’d look at the speed with which it’s changing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We would look at the whole huge array of labor market data to, to get a sense of whether conditions are really deteriorating or not.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, at the same time, we’d be looking at the other side of the mandate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We could be in a position of having to balance those two things, which is, of course, a very—a difficult balancing judgment that we’d have to make.

speaker: COLBY SMITH
sentence: On that point about balancing, I mean, you’ve mentioned that the Committee would consider how far the economy is from each goal and the time it would take to kind of get back to that point.

speaker: COLBY SMITH
sentence: But what does that mean in practice?

speaker: COLBY SMITH
sentence: I mean, how much of that assessment will be rooted in a forecast, versus data dependence?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It would be a combination of the two.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I mean, let’s just say this is a—this would be a complicated and challenging judgment that we would have to make if—and this is—we’re not in this situation, but the situation is if the two goals are in tension.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So let’s say that unemployment is moving up in an uncomfortable way and so is inflation—not the situation we’re in—hypothetically.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But we would look at how far they are from the goals, how far they’re expected to be from the goals, what’s the expected time to get back to their goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’d look at all those things and make a difficult judgment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that’s in our framework.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s always been in our thinking.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, it’s—we haven’t had—we haven’t faced that question in a very long time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so, again, difficult, difficult judgment to make, and not one that we face today.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we may never face it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, you know, we have to be keeping it in our thinking now.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Edward.

speaker: EDWARD LAWRENCE
sentence: Thank you.

speaker: EDWARD LAWRENCE
sentence: Edward Lawrence with Fox Business.

speaker: EDWARD LAWRENCE
sentence: So we had the CPI report that came out that showed, month over month, the first increase in inflation in about three years.

speaker: EDWARD LAWRENCE
sentence: The jobs report—you said “solid”—that we saw.

speaker: EDWARD LAWRENCE
sentence: At the same time, we have those new tariffs that we’re living under.

speaker: EDWARD LAWRENCE
sentence: So, given this, should the Federal Reserve be cutting rates at all this year?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, it’s going to depend.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think you have to just take a step back and realize this is—this is why we are where we are, is, you know, we are going to need to see how this evolves.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: There are cases in which it would be appropriate for us to cut rates this year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: There are cases in which it wouldn’t, and we just don’t know.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Until we know more about how this is going to settle out and what the economic implications are for employment, for—and for, for inflation, I couldn’t confidently say that I know what the appropriate path will be.

speaker: EDWARD LAWRENCE
sentence: So, following on that, just, you know—so then how does President Trump calling on you personally as well as the Federal Reserve to make rate cuts affect your decision today and affect your job difficulty?

speaker: [0:18:00] CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Doesn’t affect our—doing our job at all.

speaker: [0:18:00] CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we—you know, we’re always going to do the same thing—which is, we’re going to use our tools to foster maximum employment and price stability for the benefit of the American people.

speaker: [0:18:00] CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re always going to consider only the economic data, the outlook, the balance of risks.

speaker: [0:18:00] CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that’s it, that’s all we’re going to consider.

speaker: [0:18:00] CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So it really doesn’t affect either our job or the way we do it.

sentence: Howard.

speaker: HOWARD SCHNEIDER
sentence: Hi.

sentence: Howard Schneider with Reuters, and thanks for the time.

sentence: I’m wondering—I mean, given the complexity about the first-quarter GDP and what lies ahead, I’m just wondering what your intuition tells you about the underlying direction of the economy right now.

sentence: Many of your colleagues have said they feel growth is slowing.

sentence: If so, do you have any sense of by how much, to what degree the slowdown may be?

sentence: My gut tells me that uncertainty about the path of the economy is extremely elevated [laughter] and that the downside risks have increased.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The risk is—as we pointed out in our statement, the risks—the risks of higher unemployment and higher inflation have risen, but they haven’t materialized yet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: They really haven’t.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: They’re not, really not in the data yet, so that—and that tells me more than by intuition because I think—I think it’s obvious, actually, that the right thing for us to do is to—we’re in a good place.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Our policy’s in a very good place, and the right thing to do is, is await further clarity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I—you know, there’s—usually, things clarify, and that—the appropriate direction becomes clear.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s what usually happens, right?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Right now, it’s very hard to say what that would be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL

speaker: HOWARD SCHNEIDER
sentence: Well, let me press you on this idea of the economy being fine right now, because, reading the Beige Book very closely the last time around, there was a lot of, you know, negative stuff, negative sentiment that was in there.

speaker: HOWARD SCHNEIDER
sentence: And I know that everybody’s looking at soft data right now.

speaker: HOWARD SCHNEIDER
sentence: You mentioned it yourself—that the sentiment’s sour.

speaker: HOWARD SCHNEIDER
sentence: But the Beige Book was talking about, you know, the beginnings of layoffs in some industries, prices rising in, in some places, and an awful lot of investment decisions being, being pushed to the sideline.

speaker: HOWARD SCHNEIDER
sentence: Doesn’t that point to a slowdown?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It may well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It just hasn’t shown up yet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, and, you know, we all look at all these sentiments and read many, many individual comments just to get a better feel.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And it—you know, businesses and households very broadly are concerned and, you know, postponing economic decisions of various kinds.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, yes, if that continues and nothing, nothing happens to sort of alleviate those concerns, then you would expect that to begin to show up in economic data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It wouldn’t maybe show up overnight, but it would show up over weeks and months.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that may be what happens, but it hasn’t happened yet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And also, there are things that can happen that will—that will change that narrative.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I mean, they haven’t happened, but it’s possible to imagine things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But in the meantime, yes, we’re watching it extremely carefully, like everyone is, but don’t see really much evidence of it in the actual economic data yet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And by the way, consumers keep spending, credit card spending.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s—you know, it’s still—it’s still a healthy economy, albeit one that is shrouded in some very downbeat sentiment on the part of people and businesses.

speaker: HOWARD SCHNEIDER
sentence: Thank you.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Michael McKee.

speaker: MICHAEL MCKEE
sentence: Michael McKee from Bloomberg Radio and Television.

speaker: MICHAEL MCKEE
sentence: The Fed’s been criticized recently by a former Governor for what he calls “mission creep”—you take on more problems, use more tools, and then end up building tools to deal with the fallout of those tools, which then makes it a given that you will act more aggressively in the future.

speaker: MICHAEL MCKEE
sentence: Is that a fair critique, and is that something you would be looking at in your framework review?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Sorry, say that critique again.

speaker: MICHAEL MCKEE
sentence: That the Fed has been involved in mission creep—gets involved in using too many new tools to deal with problems and to go too far.

speaker: MICHAEL MCKEE
sentence: Is that something that—the critique was based around the fact that you did QE and QE and QE and— CHAIR POWELL.

speaker: MICHAEL MCKEE
sentence: Oh, okay.

speaker: MICHAEL MCKEE
sentence: Sure.

speaker: MICHAEL MCKEE
sentence: —and went beyond the narrow confines of your mandate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So—well, I mean, there are a couple—that’s not really beyond the confines of our mandate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I—look, I would say this: We—you know, we did things—essentially, we were on an emergency footing for a couple of years in the pandemic, and it’s very fair and very welcome for people to look back over what we did and say, “Hey, you could have done this better and different.” And one thing we hear a lot is, we could have explained the QE a little better.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We did think we were explaining it in real time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I completely accept the, the thought that we could have explained it better.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: There’s a lot of thinking that we went on too long with QE.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I can tell you that the reason we did was, we were—we were concerned that we didn’t want a tightening of—a sharp tightening in financial conditions at a time when we thought the economy was still vulnerable.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so we did hold on for a long time to QE.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we, of course, tapered and everything.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And then we immediately went into QT, and, you know, we’ve—we’re down a couple of trillion.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But I get the—that, you know, we, we certainly, with the benefit of hindsight, could have tapered earlier or faster.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s absolutely right.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But this is all very welcome.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, it’s, it’s—you know, we knew, doing this in real time, that we weren’t going to get it perfect.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And those kind of—those kind of, you know, after-action kind of looks are essential.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we’re doing the same thing in—you know, in our review, so—on some issues.

speaker: MICHAEL MCKEE
sentence: There—the other part of that critique is that you’ve taken on topics that are outside of the mandate, such as climate change and trying to ensure that certain groups are benefited by your economic policies in terms of employment, et cetera.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, okay, on climate, you’ve heard me say over and over again that we will not be climate policymakers and that our role on climate is a very, very narrow one.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I think—I think that’s what we’ve done.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’ve done really very little on climate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You can say that was—that little bit that we’ve done was too much.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But I wouldn’t want to give any impression that, that, you know, we take—that we’ve taken climate in and it’s something that we’re spending a lot of time and energy on.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re not.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We have very, very narrow things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We did one thing, one guidance for the banks, and then we did one—a one-time stress analysis, climate stress analysis, and that’s it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, you know, we dropped out of the Network for Greening the Financial System.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we didn’t do much on climate, but—and I do think, and I’ve said this publicly several times, I think it’s, it’s a real danger for us to try to take on a mandate like that, which is very narrow application to our work.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, you know, the risk is, if you—if you go for things that are really not on your mandate, you know, then why are you independent?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, I think that’s a very fair question.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I do think we’ve done a whole lot less on climate than some people seem to think we did.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Anyway, that’s what I think.

speaker: MICHAEL MCKEE
sentence: Should you have taken on the question of bringing unemployment rates down for specific categories?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We didn’t do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, we said—what we said was that we never targeted any unemployment rate for individual racial or demographic groups.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: What we said was that maximum employment was a broad and inclusive goal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I think what we meant by that was, we’re going to consider the totality of the country as we look at our maximum-employment goal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Of course, we were never going to target on any individual group with that, but I think some people, you know, wanted to hear it that way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But that’s not at all what we meant.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But—so that’s just not a correct reading of our—but I can see how, you know, maybe people found that confusing, and, you know, we have to take that into consideration.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Jo Ling.

speaker: JO LING KENT
sentence: Hi, Chair Powell.

speaker: JO LING KENT
sentence: Thanks for taking our questions today.

speaker: JO LING KENT
sentence: I’m Jo Ling Kent with CBS News.

speaker: JO LING KENT
sentence: You’ve said, “Wait and see” and “The economy is doing fine” today.

speaker: JO LING KENT
sentence: But the impact of tariffs are already showing up at the ports.

speaker: JO LING KENT
sentence: Businesses big and small are telling us that they feel it, and most importantly, consumers say they feel it.

speaker: JO LING KENT
sentence: But the challenges are here.

speaker: JO LING KENT
sentence: And there’s no waiting and seeing.

speaker: JO LING KENT
sentence: For Main Street, what is the breaking point?

speaker: JO LING KENT
sentence: What would have to happen to prompt a rate cut specifically?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Well, you know, so we really don’t see in the data yet big economic effects.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We see—we see sentiment, their concerns that higher prices may be coming, or things like that, but—so people, they’re worried now about inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: They’re worried about, you know, a shock from the tariffs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But they really haven’t—that shock hasn’t hit yet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Okay, so, you know, we’re going to be looking at not just the sentiment data, but also the real economic data as we assess what it is we should do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And remember, we’re—there will be two effects.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: One of them would be weakening economy—weakening economic activity, which translates into higher unemployment, and the other would be potentially higher inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Again, to say it again, the timing, the scope, the scale, and the persistence of those effects are very, very uncertain.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So it’s not at all clear what the appropriate response for monetary policy is at this time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we’re—you know—and by the way, our policy’s in a good place, so we think we can wait and move when it is clear what the right thing to do is; really not at all clear what it is we should do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So people are feeling stress and concern, but unemployment hasn’t gone up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Job creation is fine.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Wages are in good shape.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, people are not—layoffs are—people are not getting laid off at high levels.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, initial claims for unemployment are not increasing, you know, in any kind of impressive way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So the economy itself is still, you know, in solid shape.

speaker: JO LING KENT
sentence: Just a quick follow-up: President Trump now says he does not plan to remove you as Chair.

speaker: JO LING KENT
sentence: When you heard that, what did you think?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I don’t have anything more for you on that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I’ve pretty much covered that issue.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Thank you.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Chris.

speaker: CHRISTOPHER RUGABER
sentence: Hi.

speaker: CHRISTOPHER RUGABER
sentence: Thank you.

speaker: CHRISTOPHER RUGABER
sentence: Chris Rugaber, Associated Press.

speaker: CHRISTOPHER RUGABER
sentence: Well, I just wanted to follow up.

speaker: CHRISTOPHER RUGABER
sentence: Earlier, it sounded like you said it was unclear how the Fed—you know, what kind of interest rate decisions you will make later this year.

speaker: CHRISTOPHER RUGABER
sentence: So does that—you know, in March, there was guidance that two cuts might happen, you know, two cuts were penciled in for this year.

speaker: CHRISTOPHER RUGABER
sentence: Is that now—that guidance from the last press conference, has that been overtaken by events at this point?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, we don’t do a Summary of Economic Projections at every meeting, as you know.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We do it every other meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so this was the meeting when we didn’t do it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I—you know, we don’t also kind of poll people, so I really—I really wouldn’t want to try to make a specific projection for where we are relative to that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We will—in six weeks, we have the June meeting, and you’ll have another SEP. I’m not going to hazard a guess here today what—as to what it would be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Again, what I would say is that we think our policy rate is in a good place.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We think it leaves us well positioned to respond in a timely way to potential developments.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s where we are, and that—depending on the way things play out, that could include rate hikes—sorry, rate cuts.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, it could include us holding where we are.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We just are going to need to see, you know, how things play out before we make those decisions.

speaker: CHRISTOPHER RUGABER
sentence: Great.

speaker: CHRISTOPHER RUGABER
sentence: And just to follow up on that, I mean, when you address the issue of how the Fed would handle both rising unemployment and rising inflation, how are you thinking about the fact that addressing one could exacerbate the other?

speaker: CHRISTOPHER RUGABER
sentence: So a rate cut to reduce unemployment could worsen inflation, and vice versa.

speaker: CHRISTOPHER RUGABER
sentence: How does that—how do you handle those challenges?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Well, you just captured the—this is the issue with the two goals being in tension.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s a very challenging question.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Now, there can be a case in which one goal is very far—one variable’s very far from its goal, much farther than the other.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And if so, you concentrate on that one.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, frankly, that was the case—well, it wasn’t a case where they were really in tension.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But if you go back to 2022, it was very clear that we needed to focus on inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The labor market was also super tight, so it wasn’t really a tradeoff.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, if—I think you know what our—what our framework document says.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It says we’ll look at how far each goal—each variable is from its goal and also we’ll factor in the time it would take to get there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, you know, that’s going to be a—potentially, a very difficult judgment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But the data could break in a way that it’s not.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, I just don’t think we know that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The data could easily favor one or the other.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And right now, there’s no way to—no need to make a choice and no real basis for doing so.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Victoria.

speaker: VICTORIA GUIDA
sentence: Hi.

speaker: VICTORIA GUIDA
sentence: Victoria Guida with Politico.

speaker: VICTORIA GUIDA
sentence: I wanted to ask, Congress is currently debating spending cuts alongside expending—extending the tax cuts.

speaker: VICTORIA GUIDA
sentence: And I know you’ve talked many times about how the path of the debt is unsustainable.

speaker: VICTORIA GUIDA
sentence: But given that we’re also talking right now about the economy slowing, potentially even recession, I was just wondering, is there a danger that spending cuts now could slow growth a lot more?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, we don’t give Congress fiscal advice.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I—they’re going to do—we take what they do as a given, and we put it in our models and in our assessment of the economy, so I wouldn’t want to, you know, speculate on that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I mean, I think we do know that the debt is on an unsustainable level—on an unsustainable path—not on an unsustainable level, but an unsustainable path.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And it’s on Congress to figure out how to get us back on a sustainable path, and, you know, it’s not up to us to give them advice.

speaker: VICTORIA GUIDA
sentence: Well, do you think that they should take macroeconomic conditions into account as they look at this?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think they don’t need my advice and our advice on how to do fiscal policy any more than we need their advice on monetary policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: [Laughter] MICHELLE SMITH.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Andrew.

speaker: ANDREW ACKERMAN
sentence: Thanks, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: ANDREW ACKERMAN
sentence: Andrew Ackerman with the Washington Post.

speaker: ANDREW ACKERMAN
sentence: In your Jackson Hole comments last year, you said you would not welcome further cooling in labor market conditions.

speaker: ANDREW ACKERMAN
sentence: The unemployment rate then was 4.2 percent, which is what it is now.

speaker: ANDREW ACKERMAN
sentence: Forecasters—many forecasters now predict a higher jobless rate.

speaker: ANDREW ACKERMAN
sentence: How has your tolerance for weakening labor market conditions changed compared to a year ago?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So it was quite a different situation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: What was happening last year is that over the space of six, eight, seven months, the unemployment rate went up by almost a full percentage point, and it was click, click, click, click, click each month.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, you know, everywhere, people were talking about downside risks to the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: At the same time, payroll job numbers were getting softer and softer.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So there was a really obvious concern about downside risk to the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so at Jackson Hole and then in September, you know, we wanted to address that forthrightly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We wanted to show that we were there for the—I mean, we had been there for inflation for a couple of years, and we wanted to show also that we’re there for the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And it was important that we send that signal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Fortunately, since then, the labor market has really—and the unemployment rate have really been moving sideways at a level that is, you know, well in the range of mainstream estimates of maximum employment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that concern has gotten a lot less.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, you know, you’re at 4.2 percent unemployment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think we were in a very different situation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And now we have a situation where, you know, the risks to higher inflation and higher unemployment have both gone up, as we noted in our statement, and we’ve got to monitor both of those.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We actually have a potential situation where there may be a tradeoff or tension between the two potentially.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We don’t have it yet, and we may not have it, but that’s what we [may] have, and that’s why I think it’s a very different, different situation.

speaker: ANDREW ACKERMAN
sentence: I, I mean, I guess I want to follow up by asking how much of a rise in the jobless rate you would—you could tolerate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I can’t give you a—you know, a—I’m not going to try to give you a specific number.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I’ll just say, we’ve got—we have to now be looking at both variables and which of them is, is, you know, demanding—if one of them is demanding our focus more than the other, that would tell us what to do with policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If they’re more or less this, you know, equally distant and equally—or not distant, then we don’t have to make that assessment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, the assessment is, you wait.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I’m not going to try to be really specific about what we need to see in terms of the number.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But if—look, if we did see, you know, significant deterioration in the labor market, of course that’s one of our two variables, and we would look to be able to support that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You’d hope that it wasn’t also coming at a time when inflation was getting very bad.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, again, we’re speculating here.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We don’t know this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We don’t know any of these things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s very hypothetical.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re just going to have to wait and see how the—how it plays out.

speaker: ANDREW ACKERMAN
sentence: Thanks.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Claire.

speaker: CLAIRE JONES
sentence: Claire Jones, Financial Times.

speaker: CLAIRE JONES
sentence: In terms of getting some clarity, we’ve got some talks at the weekend in Geneva between the U.S. and China.

speaker: CLAIRE JONES
sentence: A lot of economists are ask—are attaching an awful lot of importance to how—what we hear from those talks.

speaker: CLAIRE JONES
sentence: How much importance are you attaching to them in terms of judging what will happen to the U.S. economy going forward?

speaker: CLAIRE JONES
sentence: And just in a similar vein, you know, some economists are saying it’s days, not weeks, that we have until we start to put the U.S. economy at risk of seeing a sort of pandemic here, with shortages and higher prices, if we don’t kind of soothe relations between the U.S. and China.

speaker: CLAIRE JONES
sentence: So it would be good to have your view on that, too.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, you know, these are not talks that we’re in any way involved in, so I really can’t comment directly on them.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So—but what I will say is this: You know, we had—coming out of the March meeting, we, we—the public generally had an assessment of where tariffs were going.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And then April 2 happened, and it was really substantially larger than anticipated in the forecasts that I’ve seen and in our forecast.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So—and now we—and now we have a different—we’re in a new phase where—it seems to be we’re entering a new phase where the Administration is entering into beginning talks with a number of our important trading partners.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that’s—that has the potential to change the picture materially or not.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so I think it’s going to be very important how that shakes out.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But I—you know, we simply have to wait and see how it works out.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It certainly could change the picture, and we’re mindful of not trying to make conclusive judgments about what will happen at a time when the—you know, when the facts are changing.

speaker: CLAIRE JONES
sentence: And just on the fall in shipping volumes from China over these tensions, I mean, do you share that concern that we could start seeing goods shortages and higher prices in the coming weeks if this isn’t resolved very quickly?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, I don’t want to get my—we’re not—we shouldn’t be involved, even verbally, in questions about the timing of these things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Yes, we’re—of course, we follow all that data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We see the shipping data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We see all that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, ultimately, this is for the Administration to do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: This is—you know, this is their mandate, not ours.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I know they’re—as you can see, they’re, again, having—beginning to have talks with many nations.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that has the potential to change the picture materially, so we’ll just have to wait and see.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Kosuke.

speaker: KOSUKE TAKAMI
sentence: Kosuke Takami with Nikkei.

speaker: KOSUKE TAKAMI
sentence: Thank you for doing this.

speaker: KOSUKE TAKAMI
sentence: The volume of imported goods increased significantly in the first quarter.

speaker: KOSUKE TAKAMI
sentence: Do you think the decision could cause a delay in the impact of tariff on inflation, and does this mean that it will take a longer time to reduce uncertainty?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The decision we made today?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Which decision?

speaker: KOSUKE TAKAMI
sentence: So the future decisions.

speaker: KOSUKE TAKAMI
sentence: So the volume of imports— CHAIR POWELL.

speaker: KOSUKE TAKAMI
sentence: Yes.

speaker: KOSUKE TAKAMI
sentence: —imported goods has increased significantly.

speaker: KOSUKE TAKAMI
sentence: So the impact of the imported inflation may delay.

speaker: KOSUKE TAKAMI
sentence: So, what is the impact to your future decision?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Okay, so, I mean, I think we—I think we think that the—you know, there was a big spike in imports—right?—very big, historically large, really, and—to beat tariffs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And now that should actually reverse so that it’s—you know, it’s the difference between—it’s exports minus imports, so—and imports were huge, and so then it conveyed a very negative contribution to U.S. GDP—annualized GDP in the first quarter, as we all know.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that could, in the second quarter, be reversed so that we have, you know, an unusually large contribution to—unusually positive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s very likely as imports drop sharply.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You could also have—you know, very likely you’ll have restatements of the—of the first quarter.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’ll turn out that consumer spending was higher.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It will turn out that inventories were higher.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so you’ll see—you’ll see those data revised up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It may actually go into the third quarter, too.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so I think it’s going—this whole process is going to, a little bit, make it harder to make a clean assessment of U.S. demand.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I mentioned private domestic final purchases, which doesn’t have inventories, government, or—inventories, government.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Anyway, it’s a cleaner read on private demand.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But that, that, too, probably was flattered a little bit by—you know, by strong demand for imports to be tariffed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that might overstate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s a really good reading, 3 percent PDFP in the first quarter.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That might actually overstate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So it’s not really going to—I don’t think it’s going to affect our decisions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I will just say, though, that it’s a little confusing and it’s probably less confusing to us than it would be to the general public as we try to explain this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, it’s complicated, and, you know, GDP is sending a signal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: PDFP is sending a signal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s a little bit confusing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But I think we understand what’s going, and it’s not really going to change things for us.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Courtenay.

speaker: COURTENAY BROWN
sentence: Thank you.

speaker: COURTENAY BROWN
sentence: Courtenay Brown from Axios.

speaker: COURTENAY BROWN
sentence: I guess, you know, we talked about some of the indications of potential layoffs, price hikes, an economic slowdown all being evident in the soft data.

speaker: COURTENAY BROWN
sentence: I’m curious why the Fed needs to wait for that to translate into hard data to, you know, make any type of monetary policy decision, especially if the hard data is not as timely or might be warped by tariff-related effects.

speaker: COURTENAY BROWN
sentence: Are you worried that the soft data might be some sort of false warning?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: No.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I mean, it’s—look, the—look at the state of the economies.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The labor market is solid.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Inflation is low.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We can afford to be patient as things unfold.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: There’s no real cost to our waiting at this point.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Also, the sense of it—the sense of it is, we’re not sure what the right thing will be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, there should be some increase in inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: There should be some increase in unemployment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Those call for different responses.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so until we know—potentially call for different responses—and so, you know, until we know more, we have the ability to wait and see.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And it seems to be a pretty clear decision.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Everyone on the Committee supported waiting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so that’s why we’re waiting.

speaker: COURTENAY BROWN
sentence: Just a very quick follow-up: There was this sort of vibe session, if you will, where the sentiments expressed in soft data did not translate into the hard economic data.

speaker: COURTENAY BROWN
sentence: Are you—how are you thinking about that when interpreting some of the signs in the softer survey data?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, I think, going back a number of years, the link between sentiment data and consumer spending has been weak.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s not been a strong link at all.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: On the other hand, we haven’t had a move of this, you know, speed and size.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So it wouldn’t be the case that we’re looking at this and just completely dismissing it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But it’s another reason to wait and see.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You’re right that we had a couple of years during the pandemic where people were saying—just very downbeat surveys and going out and spending money.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that can happen, and that may happen to some degree here.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We just don’t know.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: This is an outsized change in sentiment, though, and so none of us are looking at this and saying that we’re sure one way or the other.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re not.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Matt.

speaker: MATT EGAN
sentence: Thanks, Chair Powell.

speaker: MATT EGAN
sentence: Matt Egan with CNN.

speaker: MATT EGAN
sentence: So you mentioned earlier that you’re monitoring the shipping data.

speaker: MATT EGAN
sentence: And we have seen in the shipping data that imports from China into the Port of Los Angeles have plunged.

speaker: MATT EGAN
sentence: And that has raised concerns about potential shortages.

speaker: MATT EGAN
sentence: What tools, if any, does the Fed have to ensure that prices and inflation expectations don’t get out of hand if tariffs do cause significant supply chain disruptions?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I mean, we don’t have, you know, the kind of tools that are good at dealing with supply chain problems.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We don’t have that at all.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s a—that’s a job for the Administration and for the private sector more than anything.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, what we can do with our interest rate tool is, we can support—be more or less supportive of demand.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that’s—that’d be a very inefficient way to try to fix supply chain problems.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, you know, we don’t see—we don’t see the inflation yet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re, of course, reading the same stories and watching the same data as everybody else.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, you know, right now, we see inflation, you know, kind of moving sideways at a fairly low level.

speaker: MATT EGAN
sentence: If I could follow up on that, President Trump has indicated that he will likely name a replacement for you when your term as Chair expires next year.

speaker: MATT EGAN
sentence: But your position on the Board runs through January 2028, I believe.

speaker: MATT EGAN
sentence: Would you consider remaining on the Fed Board even if you’re no longer Chair?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I don’t have anything for you on that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: My whole focus is on—and my colleagues’ focus is all on, you know, trying to navigate this tricky passage we’re in right now, trying to make the right decisions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, we want to make the best decisions for the people that we serve.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s what we think about day and night.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And this is a challenging situation, and that’s, that’s 100 percent of our focus right now.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Let’s go to Jennifer for the last question.

speaker: JENNIFER SCHONBERGER
sentence: Thank you so much, Chair Powell.

speaker: JENNIFER SCHONBERGER
sentence: Jennifer Schonberger with Yahoo Finance.

speaker: JENNIFER SCHONBERGER
sentence: Public records of your schedule so far this year show no meetings with President Trump.

speaker: JENNIFER SCHONBERGER
sentence: Past Presidents Obama, Bush, and Clinton have all met with Fed Chairs.

speaker: JENNIFER SCHONBERGER
sentence: And you met with Trump during his first term.

speaker: JENNIFER SCHONBERGER
sentence: Why haven’t you asked for a meeting yet with the President?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I’ve never asked for a meeting with any President, and I never will.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s not—I wouldn’t do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: There’s never a reason for me to ask for a meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s always been the other way.

speaker: JENNIFER SCHONBERGER
sentence: So would you want to meet with him if given the opportunity— CHAIR POWELL.

speaker: JENNIFER SCHONBERGER
sentence: I never— JENNIFER SCHONBERGER.

speaker: JENNIFER SCHONBERGER
sentence: —to get more information?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I never—it’s never an initiative that I take.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s always an initiative—I—you know, I don’t think it’s up to a Fed Chair to seek a meeting with the President, although maybe some have done so.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I’ve never done so, and I can’t imagine myself doing that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s—I think it’s always—comes the other way: A President wants to meet with you.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But that hasn’t happened.

speaker: JENNIFER SCHONBERGER
sentence: And if I could just ask one question on monetary policy, when it is time to cut rates, how will you determine how far down rates will have to come to try to keep a balance on the inflation mandate as employment weakens?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, I think once you have a direction—a clear direction, you can make a—we can make a judgment about how fast to move and that kind of thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So it’s—really, the harder question is the timing, I think, and when will that become clear?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, fortunately, as I mentioned, we have our policy in a good place, the economy’s in a good place, and it’s really appropriate, we think, for us to be patient and wait for things to unfold as we get more clarity about what we should do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Thanks very much.
